scenes.tts: In 1963, with two colleagues, he asked a question no one had put precisely before: for every amino acid in a chain, which pairs of backbone angles — phi and psi — are possible without atoms colliding?
scenes.visual: 1963, three people, phi and psi, atoms colliding
scenes.narration: In 1963, with two colleagues, he asked a question no one had put precisely before: for every amino acid in a chain, which pairs of backbone angles — phi and psi — are possible without atoms colliding?

scenes.tts: They calculated the allowed distances, shaded the forbidden combinations, and plotted the result axis by axis. The survivors clustered into two compact islands — one for the alpha helix, one for the beta sheet — with the rest of the plane nearly empty.
scenes.visual: phi-psi grid: cells shaded forbidden, axes drawn, two islands labelled
scenes.narration: They calculated the allowed distances, shaded the forbidden combinations, and plotted the result axis by axis. The survivors clustered into two compact islands — one for the alpha helix, one for the beta sheet — with the rest of the plane nearly empty.

scenes.tts: Sixty years on, his plot is the first sanity check run on every new protein structure in the world. The Nobel Committee never called; the prizes that touched his field passed him by. He died in Chennai in 2001, after Parkinson's disease and the loss of his wife of fifty-three years.
